For a deterministic model, run as an ODE, Starsim can work out how each result changes as each parameter changes: the *gradient*, or the derivatives of the results with respect to the parameters. It does this by automatic differentiation with [JAX](https://docs.jax.dev), which follows the calculation of the run step by step, rather than by rerunning the model with slightly different values; the cheap steps on either side of the run (from the parameters to the numbers the run uses, and from the run to the results) are differentiated by central differences (see [the log-density](#the-log-density) for how a fit uses them). Gradients make several things possible:

- Fitting many parameters quickly, with an optimizer that follows the gradient (the default for an ODE with three or more fitted parameters).
- Drawing from the posterior (the distribution of values consistent with the data and the priors) with the No-U-Turn sampler, NUTS, a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method that uses the gradient to move through the space of parameters efficiently.
- Seeing which parts of the epidemic a parameter affects, and by how much.

This page assumes the basics of [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd). Gradients need JAX (`pip install "starsim[jax]"`), a model that runs as an ODE, and one whose whole run is compiled: a rate that calls a Python function, a module written as code, or a movement register rules them out, and the fit says which when it can't use gradients; `ss.solvers.why_not(sim, 'jax')` says so for any sim, and every reason is listed by `ss.solvers.solver_table()` (see [Solvers](architecture_solvers.qmd#what-decides-which-engine-runs-a-model)). JAX runs on a GPU if it finds one; if it can't use it (e.g. its CUDA plugin is of another version than JAX), run it on the CPU with `ss.options.jax = 'cpu'` (or the environment variable `STARSIM_JAX=cpu`) before it is first used.

## The model

The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune, with two unknowns: the transmission rate `beta` and the share of cases reported, `report`. Reported cases are counts, so their likelihood is a Poisson: it says how the data vary around the model's value. The data are a year of weekly cases drawn from a run with `beta = 1.9` and `report = 0.5`:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])  # Transmission rate per day
report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1]) # Share of cases reported

infection = S >> E @ beta*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
cases     = ss.outcome(report*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson())
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')
```

## The gradient of a result

`sim.gradient()` gives the derivative of each result, at each time, with respect to each parameter with bounds, at the parameters' current values. Here, at the true values, for the daily reported cases:

```{python}
grad = truth.gradient('cases')

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
t = truth.results.timevec
ax.plot(t, grad.beta.measles.cases, label='Change in daily cases per unit of beta')
ax.plot(t, grad.report.measles.cases, label='Change in daily cases per unit of report')
ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5)
ax.legend();
```

A higher β brings the epidemic forward: more cases before the peak, and fewer after it, when the susceptible people have already been used up. A higher reporting share scales every week's cases up in proportion. Because the two parameters change the curve in different ways, the data can tell them apart. Two parameters whose gradients had the same shape could only be fitted as a combination (see [Parameter identification](calibration_identification.qmd)).

The result is indexed by parameter, then module, then result: `grad.beta.measles.cases` is an array with one value per time step.

`sim.gradient()` also takes a function of the run sim, which can be anything that returns a number or an array, e.g. a total cost. Its gradient is worked out from the same run in JAX, so it needs no JAX of your own:

```{python}
total = lambda sim: sim.results.measles.cases.sum()
truth.gradient(total)
```

## Many values

A parameter with a value for each level of a stratification (`ss.par(ss.by(patch=[...]), bounds=...)`), an array, or a time series has a gradient for each value, named as a fit names them. A time series fitted value by value is a way to estimate a transmission rate that changes in time, with no shape assumed for it. Here the data come from an outbreak whose transmission rate fell by about a third over June (as it might when schools close for the summer), and the rate is fitted as a value every four weeks, with straight lines between them:

```{python}
start = ss.date(pars['start'])
true_beta = ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': 1.9, '2025-05-31': 1.9, '2025-06-30': 1.2}, 'linear') # 1.9 until the end of May, then falling to 1.2 by the end of June
dates = [start + ss.days(d) for d in range(0, 365, 28)] # A value every four weeks, in between which it changes linearly
beta = ss.par(ss.timeseries(dates, [1.5]*len(dates), 'linear'), bounds=[0.5, 4])

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
onset = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson()) # The share reported, taken as known here
measles_t = ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
truth_t = ss.Sim(measles_t, pars=dict(beta=true_beta), rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars).run()
data_t = truth_t.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

smooth = lambda pars: 100*np.sum(np.diff(pars['beta'].values)**2) # Large changes from one value to the next are unlikely
fit_t = ss.Sim(measles_t, data=data_t, **pars).fit(penalty=smooth, verbose=False)

days = lambda times: [(ss.date(t) - start).days for t in times] # Days since the start
t = np.arange(365)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, np.interp(t, days(true_beta.times), true_beta.values), 'k--', label='True')
ax.plot(days(fit_t.pars.beta.times), fit_t.pars.beta.values, 'o-', label='Fitted')
ax.set_xlabel('Days since 1 January 2025')
ax.set_ylabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend();
```

The fit finds the fall, and its size, from the weekly cases alone. It is more gradual than the truth, beginning a few weeks before it and ending a few weeks after, since the penalty (`penalty=`) keeps each value close to its neighbors, and the values are four weeks apart. Without the penalty, the values early in the year, when there are few cases, would wander, since the data say little about them. A larger penalty gives a smoother curve that is slower to follow a change; a smaller one, a curve that follows the noise.

With many values, what the fit minimizes is differentiated in reverse mode, which takes one pass whatever the number of values, and a long run is checkpointed so that the memory it takes grows only as the square root of its length. Neither is a setting.

## The log-density

`sim.log_density()` gives the log of the posterior density of the fitted parameters (the log-likelihood of the data, plus the log of the priors), as a function of their values, together with its gradient. It is what a sampler or optimizer of your own would use. Besides calling it (`density(x)`) and its gradient (`density.grad(x)`), `density.fn` is the function itself, to compose with JAX (`jax.vmap`, `jax.hessian`, ...), and `density.run(x)` gives the number in each state at each time at those values:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
density = sim.log_density()
print('Parameters:', density.names)
print('At the starting values:', density.x0)
print('Log-density:', density(density.x0))
print('Its gradient:', density.grad(density.x0))
```

The gradient is positive for both parameters: at the starting values (1.5 and 0.3), increasing either would make the data more likely.

The log-density is one function of the values, which has to hold over the whole of the bounds, not only where it was built. The rates in the model are worked out in JAX from the model's own expressions, so they are exact at any values. The other numbers that depend on the fitted parameters (the initial number in each state, the shares of a transition that branches, and inflows) are taken as linear in them, from how they change at the starting values. That is checked when the log-density is built, at the corners and the middle of the bounds, and a model where they aren't linear (e.g. an initial number that is the product of two fitted parameters) is an error that names them: then the default fit uses Nelder-Mead, and NUTS or L-BFGS-B need `require_jax=False`, which takes the gradients with Python in the loop. The same log-density is what L-BFGS-B and NUTS use in a fit with a likelihood.

## A best fit with gradients

`sim.fit()` uses the gradient by default when a deterministic model has three or more fitted parameters (`'l-bfgs-b'`); with one or two, Nelder–Mead, which needs no gradient, is faster. Either can be asked for:

```{python}
fit = sim.fit(method='l-bfgs-b')
fit.table
```

Every data series here has a likelihood, so this is the maximum likelihood estimate. If a parameter has a prior (`ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4], prior=ss.normal(2, 0.2))`), the best fit is instead the most probable value, given the data and the prior.

## A posterior with NUTS

A best fit is one set of values. A posterior is the whole distribution of values that are consistent with the data, which says how certain each value is, and how the parameters depend on each other. `method='nuts'` draws from it, given a likelihood for every data series. The priors are each parameter's `prior=`, or uniform over its bounds:

```{python}
post = sim.fit(method=ss.fit.method('nuts', draws=250, warmup=250))
post.summarize();
```

Each chain of the sampler starts from a draw near one of the best optima found from a scan (from the Laplace approximation there, made twice as wide in variance, so that the chains start apart and R-hat can see whether they come together), spends `warmup=` draws tuning itself, and then makes `draws=` draws (500 of each by default; fewer here to keep this page quick). The table gives, for each parameter, the median of the posterior and its 95% interval (`lower` and `upper`), with two checks that the chains agree: the R-hat (`rhat`), which should be at most 1.01, and the effective sample size (`ess`), the number of independent draws the correlated draws are worth. [Fit diagnostics](calibration_diagnostics.qmd) says what to do if they fail.

The draws themselves are in `post.samples`, one row for each:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(post.samples.beta, post.samples.report, s=5, alpha=0.5)
ax.scatter(1.9, 0.5, marker='x', s=100, color='red', label='True values')
ax.set_xlabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylabel('report')
ax.legend();
```

The two are negatively correlated: a slightly higher β gives a slightly larger epidemic, which a slightly lower reporting share brings back to the same number of reported cases.

The posterior is narrow because the data were made by this very ODE, with Poisson noise, so the likelihood describes their noise exactly. Real counts vary more than that, and a real outbreak has chance in its transmission that an ODE leaves out. With a Poisson likelihood, the posterior of real data would be as narrow as this one and wrong: [Fitting methods](calibration_methods.qmd#comparing-the-methods) shows an ODE's posterior excluding the true values of data from a stochastic model. A negative binomial likelihood with its dispersion fitted (`likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=ss.par(10, bounds=[1, 100], name='dispersion')))`) lets the data say how variable they are, and widens the posterior to match, as in [T7](../tutorials/t7_calibration.qmd#how-sure-is-the-fit); for chance in transmission, use a stochastic model and `method='pmcmc'`.

## Profile likelihoods

A profile likelihood is another way to find a confidence interval for one parameter, without priors: at each value of it, the other parameters are refitted, and the values whose negative log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the lowest form the 95% confidence interval. It also shows whether the data determine the parameter at all: a profile that stays flat up to a bound means they don't.

```{python}
prof = ss.fit.profile(sim, 'beta', values=np.linspace(1.86, 1.94, 9))
print('Best value of beta:', round(prof.best, 3))
print('95% confidence interval:', np.round(prof.interval, 3))
prof.table
```

Without `values=`, `ss.fit.profile()` chooses the values itself, spread over the bounds and then concentrated around the best, which takes longer. Plotting the profile:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(prof.table.beta, prof.table.nll - prof.table.nll.min(), 'o-')
ax.axhline(prof.threshold, color='k', ls='--', label='95% threshold')
ax.set_xlabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylabel('Negative log-likelihood, above the lowest')
ax.legend();
```

The interval agrees with the posterior's above. A profile needs a deterministic model whose data series all have a likelihood, and parameters without priors.

## Projecting from a posterior

`fit.project()` runs the fitted model under each scenario, once for each of `n_runs` draws from the posterior, with the same draws (and seeds) in every scenario. Each draw has a seed of its own, so the spread of the runs is the uncertainty in the fitted values, carried into the projection, together with chance. Here, a catch-up campaign on 1 April, before the peak, that vaccinates half of those still susceptible, compared with none:

```{python}
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.97, who=measles.S, when='2025-04-01', coverage=0.5)
proj = post.project({'No campaign': None, 'Campaign': vaccination}, n_runs=50)
proj.plot('measles.cases')
```

```{python}
proj.summarize().loc['measles_cases']
```

Since the model is deterministic, each run differs only in its parameter values, so the interval is the uncertainty from the fit alone. For a stochastic model, the runs would also differ by chance, and with particle MCMC each continues a run that follows the data (see [Projecting from a posterior](calibration_fitting.qmd#projecting-from-a-posterior)).

The same draws show the fit against the data: the model's weekly cases at the starting values and at the best values, with 95% of the posterior as a band:

```{python}
post.plot()
```

## Other samplers

NUTS is for deterministic models. For a stochastic model, the likelihood can't be differentiated, and the other posterior methods apply (see [Fitting a model](calibration_fitting.qmd#how-the-fit-is-found)):

- `method='pmcmc'`, particle MCMC, for a stochastic compartmental model (e.g. `solver='binomial'`) whose data series all have a likelihood: the likelihood at each point is estimated by running many copies of the model (particles) and weighting them by how well they match each data point. For an ODE that JAX can't run, `'pmcmc'` is a random walk on its exact likelihood, which needs no gradients.
- `method='abc-smc'`, approximate Bayesian computation, for any stochastic model, including agents: it keeps the values whose runs come closest to the data, and needs no likelihood; its result is an approximation, whose width depends on how small its tolerance became.
- `method='if2'`, iterated filtering, finds the maximum likelihood values of a stochastic compartmental model with particles.

Starsim's samplers can also be used directly, for a log-density of your own (such as `density` above): `ss.fit.nuts()`, `ss.fit.pmmh()` (a random-walk Metropolis sampler, as particle MCMC uses), and `ss.fit.abc_smc()`; see [ss.fit](../api/fit.qmd).

A posterior can also be put together by hand, by sampling-importance resampling, which needs only runs of the model and a likelihood: draw many sets of values from the priors and run each (`ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=1000)`, whose `msim.runs` has the values of each run), work out the likelihood of the data for each run (`ss.fit.loglik(run)`), and resample the runs in proportion to their likelihoods. It is simple and works for any model, but most draws from a wide prior land where the likelihood is negligible, so it needs many runs for few parameters, and fails for many.

How the gradients are computed (the run in JAX, and the steps around it) is explained in [Randomness](architecture_randomness.qmd#randomness-in-fitting).

## Further reading

- [JAX: Automatic differentiation](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/automatic-differentiation.html): how the gradients of a run are worked out
- [Stan: User's guide](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/index.html): Bayesian fitting with NUTS, including ODE models
- [NumPyro: Getting started](https://num.pyro.ai/en/stable/getting_started.html): another implementation of NUTS in JAX, for models written as Python functions
- [Grinsztajn et al. (2021): Bayesian workflow for disease transmission modeling in Stan](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8661657/): fitting an SIR model with NUTS, step by step
